ch04.anchor: worked his way inside the enemy secret service in Guisui
ch04.note: Guisui was the name of the city now called Hohhot, capital of Inner Mongolia; under Japanese occupation it was renamed Houhehaote. It was the seat of the Suiyuan provincial government and the focus of much of the intelligence work in this chapter (printed folio 136).

ch04.anchor: the Guisui Investigation and Statistics office
ch04.note: The “Investigation and Statistics” (diaotong) organs were the provincial arm of the Kuomintang party’s intelligence and counter-intelligence system, parallel to the Central Statistics Bureau (Zhongtong) at the center. The book uses the term for the Suiyuan provincial secret police that hunted Communist agents (printed folio 136).

A Communist-led patriotic youth organization (the “Vanguard,” Minxian) founded in Beiping in 1936; it drew students into the anti-Japanese movement and served as a recruiting ground for the Party (printed folio 136).

A training school for young patriots run at Anwubao, in Jingyang County, Shaanxi, on the edge of the Communist border region; nominally a Nationalist youth camp, it was in practice a Communist cadre school in the late 1930s (printed folio 136).

The Shanxi Sacrifice for National Salvation League (Xisheng jiuguo tongmenghui, or Ximeng Hui), a mass anti-Japanese body set up under Yan Xishan in 1936 but heavily penetrated and led by Communists (printed folio 136).

So printed; plainly a misprint for 1942. The training class at Zaoyuan in Yan’an belongs to the 1940s, and the narrative has just placed Zhang He in the Shaan-Gan-Ning region in 1941 (printed folio 136).
The liangmin zheng, an identity pass issued to civilians in Japanese-occupied areas; carrying a proper one was essential to move through checkpoints (printed folio 137).

ch04.anchor: the puppet Houhehaote city post office
ch04.note: Houhehaote (from the Mongolian name of the city) was the name imposed on Guisui under the Japanese-sponsored Mongol regime; “puppet” marks the occupation administration (printed folio 137).

ch04.anchor: During the First Suiyuan Campaign in November 1945
ch04.note: The Communist offensive of October–December 1945 that besieged Guisui and Baotou in the opening months of the civil war; it failed to take either city (printed folio 138).

ch04.anchor: the security system of the Jin-Ji district of Jin-Cha-Ji
ch04.note: Jin-Cha-Ji (Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei) was one of the great Communist base areas of north China; “Jin-Ji” denotes its Shanxi-Hebei sub-region (printed folio 138).
A Japanese secret-service organ operating under an economic-survey cover in occupied Shanxi; after the surrender Yan Xishan took it over, keeping some of its Japanese staff (printed folio 141).

Gao Kelin (1907–1989), a veteran Communist then heading the Party’s Saibei district committee and its Social Affairs Department (intelligence and security); later a senior judicial official of the People’s Republic (printed folio 139).

ch04.anchor: The director of the Yanbei office was Chu Xichun
ch04.note: Chu Xichun (1896–1966), a Yan Xishan general who in 1949 took part in the peaceful handover of Beiping and served the People’s Republic thereafter (printed folio 141).

ch04.anchor: the Ministry of State Security set up a leading group
ch04.note: The PRC Ministry of State Security, formed in 1983 by merging the counter-intelligence work of the Ministry of Public Security with the Party’s Investigation Department; in 1985 it gathered veterans like Chen Yangshan to record the history of the hidden front (printed folio 142).

Lu Nan was the codename of Zhao Xihong (also called Zhao Fumin), the agent whose network this section follows; the name echoes his Shandong birthplace (Lu is the classical name for Shandong). He is not to be confused with the southern-Shandong region (printed folio 143).

ch04.anchor: He Shaonan's security-command headquarters at Suide
ch04.note: He Shaonan was the Kuomintang commissioner and security commander of the Suide district on the Shaan-Gan-Ning border; his clashes with the Communists ended when he was driven out in 1940 (printed folio 143).
Chen Qihan (1897–1981), a senior Red Army and later PLA commander, made a general in 1955 and president of the PLA Military Court (printed folio 143).

ch04.anchor: the Ike Zhao League of Suiyuan province
ch04.note: The Ike Zhao League (Yeke Juu) was the Mongol banner-league of the Ordos region, in the great southern bend of the Yellow River; it is now the city of Ordos (printed folio 143).
Ma Zhanshan (1885–1950), the general famed for defying orders and fighting the Japanese in Manchuria in 1931–32; by this time he commanded cavalry in the northwest (printed folio 144).

ch04.anchor: the third class of the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University
ch04.note: The Anti-Japanese Military and Political University (Kangda), the Communists’ chief training academy at Yan’an, which turned out military and political cadres in successive classes through the war (printed folio 144).

ch04.anchor: Here were Chen Changjie's Ike Zhao League Garrison Command
ch04.note: Chen Changjie (1892–1968), a Yan Xishan and later Nationalist general; he commanded the defense of Tianjin and was captured when the city fell in January 1949 (printed folio 144).

Juntong (the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission) was the Nationalists’ military secret service under Dai Li, distinct from the party’s Central Statistics Bureau (Zhongtong); the rivalry between the two runs through this section. After 1946 Juntong was reorganized as the Bureau of Confidential Investigation (printed folio 144).

ch04.anchor: On the eve of the Party's Seventh Congress in 1945
ch04.note: The Chinese Communist Party’s Seventh National Congress, held at Yan’an from April to June 1945, which enshrined Mao Zedong Thought and set the line for the final drive to power (printed folio 145).

Ma Hansan, the Juntong chief in the northwest, was himself arrested and shot by his own service in 1948 for embezzlement, including the theft of a jeweled Qing seal; the source elsewhere spells his name Ma Hanshan (printed folio 145).

ch04.anchor: an introductory document signed by Ouyang Qin
ch04.note: Ouyang Qin (1900–1978), a senior Communist then in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region Security Office, later first Party secretary of Heilongjiang (printed folio 146).

ch04.anchor: to defect through contact with Dong Qiwu
ch04.note: The source appends a biographical footnote here: Dong Qiwu (1899–1989) joined the army in 1919 and served through the Northern Expedition; from 1928 he rose under Fu Zuoyi as staff officer, regimental and brigade commander; he fought at the Great Wall in 1933 and helped organize the 1936 Suiyuan resistance. In 1949 he led the Suiyuan peaceful uprising; in 1951 he commanded the 23rd Corps of the Chinese People’s Volunteers in Korea, and in 1955 was made a general. He joined the Communist Party in 1980 and died in 1989 (printed folio 148).

The Suiyuan fangshi, the Party’s policy of leaving Suiyuan’s Nationalist forces in place under a standing truce until they could be brought over peacefully rather than crushed; it produced Dong Qiwu’s bloodless uprising of September 1949 (printed folio 148).

Zhou Fohai (1897–1948), a founder of the Communist Party who defected to the Kuomintang and then became a leading minister in Wang Jingwei’s Japanese-sponsored government; he died in prison after the war (printed folio 151).
Chen Gongbo (1892–1946), another founding Communist turned Nationalist, who succeeded Wang Jingwei as head of the puppet regime at Nanjing; he was tried and executed in 1946 (printed folio 151).

ch04.anchor: After the Shangdang Campaign of January 1945
ch04.note: So dated in the source, but in error: the Shangdang Campaign, in which Yan Xishan lost some thirteen divisions, was fought in September and October 1945. The reorganization it forced is the same one described in section 4 (printed folio 153).

ch04.anchor: an army doctor in He Zhuguo's 2nd Cavalry Army
ch04.note: He Zhuguo (1897–1985), a cavalry general of the Northeastern Army; naming him lent Zheng Gui’s cover story a plausible wartime record (printed folio 156).
Mao Renfeng (1898–1956), who took over the Nationalist secret service after Dai Li’s death in 1946 and ran the Bureau of Confidential Investigation through the civil war (printed folio 158).
The gold yuan (jinyuan quan), the currency the Nationalist government issued in August 1948 to replace the collapsing fabi; it too collapsed within months in runaway inflation (printed folio 158).

The jiaozong, the Nationalist regional command charged with “suppressing bandits,” their term for the Communists; the North China headquarters under Fu Zuoyi directed the defense of the Beiping-Tianjin region (printed folio 158).
On September 19, 1949, Dong Qiwu led the Nationalist forces and administration of Suiyuan to defect to the Communists without a fight, the culmination of the “Suiyuan formula” (printed folio 160).
